name: Chhoser
tagline: Sky caves and cliff monasteries north of the walled city
meta_description: Chhoser near Lo Manthang: the Jhong cave complex, Garphu and Nyiphu cliff gompas and the Mustang sky caves, reached on a half-day ride from the walled city.
summary: Chhoser is a small Loba village at about 3,900 m in a valley north-east of Lo Manthang, known for its cliffs riddled with man-made caves. Its Jhong cave complex, several levels of rooms cut into the rock, is the easiest place in Mustang to step inside a sky cave, and the cliff gompas of Garphu and Nyiphu stand nearby.
intro: Ride or drive north-east from Lo Manthang for an hour or so and the valley narrows between cliffs of soft, banded rock. Look up and you see rows of dark openings high on the cliff faces, sometimes five or six storeys of them, like the windows of an abandoned building. These are the sky caves of Mustang, dug by hand into the cliffs centuries ago, and around Chhoser they are more numerous than almost anywhere else in Lo.

Chhoser itself is a small farming village of whitewashed houses, barley fields and willow trees along the stream. Its best-known site is the Jhong cave, a complex of rooms cut into the cliff on several levels and linked by passages and ladders, which visitors can enter with a ticket. Close by, two small monasteries, Garphu and Nyiphu, are built against the cliffs, partly in caves themselves, with old paintings and resident caretakers.

We usually visit Chhoser as a half-day or full-day trip from Lo Manthang, on horseback or by jeep, combining the Jhong cave, one or both of the cliff gompas and a picnic lunch in the valley. It is the best place in Upper Mustang to understand the cave story, which runs from burials made around 3,000 years ago to meditation cells used by monks in the 15th century and later.

story.title: Ten thousand caves and the people who made them
paras: Across Mustang there are some 10,000 man-made caves dug into the walls of valleys, many of them in Upper Mustang near the Kali Gandaki and its side streams. No one is quite sure who first made them or why. Archaeologists divide their use into three broad periods. As early as about 1,000 BC some were used as burial chambers. Around the 10th century, when the region was often fought over, families moved into the caves for safety, turning them into homes. By the 1400s, many had become meditation chambers and storerooms for monasteries.

Since the 1990s, teams of Nepali and foreign archaeologists, mountaineers and conservators have climbed into caves across Lo. In the mid-1990s, researchers from Nepal and the University of Cologne found partially mummified human remains at least 2,000 years old. In 2007 a team found Buddhist paintings and manuscripts in caves near Lo Manthang, and in 2010, at Samdzong, near the Tibetan border, archaeologists found 27 skeletons from the 3rd to 8th centuries with cut marks on the bones, probably from a burial ritual.

Chhoser, once known as Garphu, was a village development committee of its own until 2017, when it became part of Lomanthang rural municipality. Its caves have long been part of village life, used for storage and shelter within living memory. Today the Jhong cave is managed for visitors, the cliff gompas are kept by caretakers, and the village farms barley and keeps animals as before. The caves on the higher cliffs remain out of reach, and most are still unexplored.

people: Chhoser's families are Loba, speaking Lo-ke and Nepali and following the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism. They farm barley, buckwheat and potatoes, keep yaks, goats and horses, and some trade along the road to the Tibetan border at Korala. A few families earn income from the Jhong cave tickets, horse hire and tea for visitors. As in the rest of Lo, many people spend winter further south.

untold.fact: Mustang's caves are thought to have been used as burial chambers as early as about 1,000 BC, as homes from around the 10th century and as meditation chambers by the 1400s. The cave sites have been on UNESCO's tentative list since 1996.

In 2010 a team of mountaineers and archaeologists recovered the remains of 27 people from two caves near Samdzong in Upper Mustang, dated to the 3rd–8th centuries, with cut marks on the bones linked to a burial ritual.
Chhoser, also known as Garphu, was a separate village development committee with 728 people at the 1991 census, and was merged into Lomanthang rural municipality in 2017.

taste.name: Chhurpi
taste.text: Chhurpi is dried cheese made from yak or cow milk, cut into small, very hard cubes that you suck slowly for an hour or more. Families around Chhoser make it, and it is sold in Lo Manthang. A good snack to carry on the ride to the caves.

facts: Half day to 1 day from Lo Manthang
Flight to Jomsom via Pokhara, jeep to Lo Manthang, then ≈ 1 h by jeep or horse
Jhong cave complex, sky caves, Garphu and Nyiphu cliff gompas

highlights.title: Jhong cave
highlights.text: A multi-level complex of rooms cut into the cliff, with dozens of chambers linked by narrow passages, holes and ladders. Climb carefully with a torch and imagine the families or monks who lived here. A small ticket is collected at the entrance.

highlights.title: Garphu gompa
highlights.text: A small monastery built against the cliff in the Chhoser valley, partly using caves as rooms. Old statues and paintings, and a caretaker who opens it for visitors. Its setting, with cave mouths in the rock above, is unlike any other gompa in Lo.

highlights.title: Nyiphu gompa
highlights.text: A second cliff monastery near Garphu, small and quiet, with its own shrine room in the rock. Visiting both makes a good morning with the Jhong cave. Leave a donation at each and ask before taking photographs inside.

highlights.title: The cave cliffs
highlights.text: All along the valley, the cliffs are pitted with rows of caves, some high above any reachable ground. The best light for photography comes in the early morning and late afternoon, when shadows bring out the openings.

highlights.title: Ride from Lo Manthang
highlights.text: Most visitors come on horseback from Lo Manthang, about 1.5–2 hours each way over open plain and into the valley, with local handlers leading. A slower and far more rewarding way to arrive than by jeep.

how_to_reach.text: Chhoser is about 1 hour by jeep north-east of Lo Manthang on rough tracks. Jeeps can be hired in Lo Manthang for a half-day trip. From Jomsom it is a long day's drive; most people base themselves in Lo Manthang. Check current road status locally.
Walk from Lo Manthang in about 3 hours each way across the plain and up the valley, or ride a horse in 1.5–2 hours with a local handler. Many visitors ride out and walk part of the way back.

where_to_stay: Chhoser has very few facilities for overnight visitors, and we do not plan nights here. Stay in Lo Manthang, where family-run lodges inside and just outside the city walls offer heated dining rooms and simple rooms, and visit Chhoser as a half-day or full-day trip. Carry a packed lunch, water and snacks from your lodge; there may be tea available at the Jhong cave or in the village, but do not rely on it. In Lo Manthang, book well ahead for May and October.
tips: Bring a head torch to explore the Jhong cave; the inner rooms are dark and the passages uneven.
Wear shoes with good grip and keep hands free; you climb ladders and squeeze through narrow openings.
Do not try to climb to caves on the cliff faces; the rock is soft and unstable.
Carry cash for cave tickets and gompa donations, and a packed lunch from Lo Manthang.
Start early to avoid the strong afternoon wind on the open plain between Lo Manthang and Chhoser.

experiences.title: Climb through the Jhong cave complex
experiences.summary: Step inside one of Mustang's sky caves at Chhoser's Jhong cave, a multi-level complex of rooms cut into the cliff and linked by passages and ladders. The easiest and safest way to understand how people lived and worshipped in these caves for centuries.
body: The Jhong cave sits in the cliff above the Chhoser valley, its entrance reached by a short climb from the path. A caretaker collects a small ticket. Inside, rooms have been cut into the soft rock on several levels, linked by narrow passages, holes in the floors and ceilings, and wooden ladders. Some rooms have niches, hearths and smoke-blackened ceilings that show people once lived here. Small windows look out over the valley.

Your guide explains what the caves were used for over time: burials in the earliest periods, homes when the region was unsafe, and later meditation cells and storerooms for monasteries. Some caves elsewhere in Mustang have yielded paintings, manuscripts and human remains, but the Jhong cave has long been open and is now mostly empty, which makes it easier to imagine daily life in its rooms. Look for tool marks on the walls where the rock was cut by hand.

The climb inside is not hard, but it is cramped, dusty and dark in places. A head torch is essential, and you need both hands free for the ladders. People who dislike tight spaces may prefer to see only the lower levels. Allow an hour or so, then sit outside at the entrance and look across the valley at the hundreds of other caves still out of reach. It is a quiet, thoughtful place.

faqs.q: What is the Jhong cave in Mustang?
faqs.a: The Jhong cave is a multi-level cave complex cut into the cliffs at Chhoser, north-east of Lo Manthang. It has dozens of rooms linked by passages, holes and ladders. It is one of the few Mustang sky caves open to visitors, with a small ticket. It gives a clear idea of how such caves were used as homes and retreats.

faqs.q: Is the Jhong cave safe for children?
faqs.a: Older children who are comfortable with ladders and tight spaces usually enjoy it, with an adult close by. Very young children may find it difficult, and the drop from some openings is a hazard. Keep them close, use head torches and do not let anyone lean out of the windows. Your guide can advise on the day.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to enter the Jhong cave?
faqs.a: There is a small entry fee for visitors, paid to the caretaker at the entrance, in Nepali rupees. The fee changes from time to time and may be different for foreigners and Nepalis. Carry small notes. The money helps maintain the site and supports the village. Check current fees locally.

experiences.title: The cliff gompas of Garphu and Nyiphu
experiences.summary: Visit two small monasteries built against the cliffs of the Chhoser valley, Garphu and Nyiphu, partly using the caves as shrine rooms. Old statues, faded paintings and quiet caretakers, in one of the most unusual monastic settings in Upper Mustang.
body: Garphu and Nyiphu stand in the Chhoser valley not far from the Jhong cave, each built against the base of the cliff so that the rock forms part of the building. Above them, the cliff is pitted with caves, some once used as meditation cells by monks and hermits. The setting shows the link between the caves and the religious life of Lo, which continued for centuries after people stopped living in them.

At each gompa your guide finds the caretaker, who opens the shrine rooms. Inside are statues, butter lamps, painted walls and texts, darkened by age and smoke. Some of the rooms run back into the rock, cool and dim. Remove your shoes, walk clockwise and ask before taking photographs; some caretakers allow pictures without flash, others prefer none at all. Look for old offerings left in rock niches, and the soot marks of centuries of butter lamps on the ceilings.

The two gompas are small and quiet, and it is easy to spend time simply sitting in the courtyard and watching the light on the cliffs. Leave a donation at each, NPR 300–500 per person is appropriate, to support the caretakers. Combine the gompas with the Jhong cave in a single morning, then ride back to Lo Manthang for a late lunch before the afternoon wind. It is a peaceful end to the morning.

faqs.q: What are Garphu and Nyiphu?
faqs.a: Garphu and Nyiphu are two small monasteries in the Chhoser valley north-east of Lo Manthang, built against the cliffs and partly using caves as rooms. They are looked after by caretakers and still used for worship. Visiting them with the nearby Jhong cave shows how caves and monasteries were linked in Lo.

faqs.q: Can I visit Garphu and Nyiphu without a guide?
faqs.a: In practice, no. You need a licensed guide for Upper Mustang under the restricted area permit rules, and the guide's local contacts are needed to find the caretakers, who hold the keys. Without them, you are likely to find the gompas locked. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does it take to visit the Chhoser monasteries?
faqs.a: Allow about two hours for both gompas, including the short walks between them and time with the caretakers. Combined with the Jhong cave and travel from Lo Manthang by horse or jeep, a visit to Chhoser takes a long half day or a relaxed full day. Start early to avoid the afternoon wind.

experiences.title: Ride a Mustang horse to Chhoser
experiences.summary: Leave Lo Manthang at dawn on a sturdy Mustang horse and ride across the open plain and into the Chhoser valley, with its cave-pitted cliffs, the Jhong cave and two cliff gompas, before riding back in the afternoon. The classic day trip from the walled city.
body: Horses are part of everyday life in Lo, and riding is the traditional way to travel between villages. We arrange horses and local handlers through families in Lo Manthang. The horses are small, strong and sure-footed, and the handlers lead them on steep or loose ground, so riding experience is not needed. We set off soon after sunrise, when the plain is calm and the light is soft. Dress warmly for the first hour.

The ride out takes about 1.5–2 hours across the open plain north-east of the city and into the Chhoser valley, where the cliffs close in and the caves appear above you. We stop at the Jhong cave and the gompas of Garphu and Nyiphu, and have a packed lunch by the stream. The handlers rest the horses and often know the caretakers personally. It is a relaxed, unhurried day with plenty of stops.

We ride back in the early afternoon, ideally before the strongest wind picks up on the plain. Total riding time is about 4 hours, which is a lot in a traditional saddle; bring padded trousers or a folded fleece to sit on. Wear sunglasses, sunscreen and a buff for dust. If you prefer, a jeep can take you one way and the horse the other. Tip the handlers at the end of the day.

faqs.q: How long is the horse ride from Lo Manthang to Chhoser?
faqs.a: About 1.5–2 hours each way, so 3–4 hours in the saddle for the round trip, plus time at the Jhong cave and gompas. Most visitors make it a full day, leaving early and returning in mid-afternoon. A jeep can shorten the trip to about an hour each way if you prefer.

faqs.q: Are the horses in Upper Mustang safe for beginners?
faqs.a: Yes. Horses hired out in Lo Manthang are used to visitors and to the terrain, and a local handler walks alongside, leading the horse on steep sections. The main discomforts are the hard traditional saddle and the wind. Helmets are not standard, so bring your own if you want one.

faqs.q: Can I combine horse and jeep for Chhoser?
faqs.a: Yes. Many visitors ride out to Chhoser in the calm morning and take a jeep back to Lo Manthang, or the other way round. This reduces time in the saddle and avoids riding into the afternoon wind. We arrange the horse and jeep the evening before through families in Lo Manthang.

experiences.title: Walk the cave cliffs of the Chhoser valley
experiences.summary: A gentle walk along the floor of the Chhoser valley beneath cliffs pitted with rows of man-made caves, with a guide who explains the geology, the history of the caves and the finds made in similar caves across Upper Mustang. Best in low light for photographs.
body: From Chhoser village we walk along the stream through fields and willows, with the valley walls rising on either side. The cliffs are made of soft sedimentary rock in bands of grey, cream and ochre, easy to dig but quick to erode. Along them run rows of dark openings, some within reach, many high and long cut off as the cliff faces have retreated. Your guide will help you pick out stacked caves, linked by internal passages.

As we walk, the guide tells the story of the caves of Mustang, about 10,000 of them across the district: burial chambers 2,000–3,000 years ago, homes in unsettled times, meditation cells and libraries later. Since the 1990s, teams of archaeologists and climbers have found human remains, Buddhist paintings and manuscripts in caves across Upper Mustang, though many caves remain unexplored. Every cave you see has a story still waiting to be told, and the guide will share what is known.

The walk is easy, mostly flat and about 2–3 hours at a slow pace. In the early morning or late afternoon, low light picks out the cave openings in sharp shadow, the best time for photographs. Do not attempt to climb to any cave; the rock is unstable and the sites are fragile heritage. Carry water, sun protection and warm layers, since the valley can be cold in shade. Binoculars help.

faqs.q: Who made the caves in Mustang?
faqs.a: No one knows exactly. The caves were dug by hand into soft cliffs over many centuries, by people whose identity is still studied. Archaeologists have found that some were used as burial chambers as early as about 1,000 BC, others as homes from around the 10th century, and later as meditation cells and storerooms for monasteries.

faqs.q: Can I climb into the sky caves around Chhoser?
faqs.a: Only the Jhong cave and a few other managed caves are open to visitors. The high caves on the cliff faces are dangerous to reach, as the rock is soft and crumbling, and they are fragile archaeological sites. Climbing to them without permission and proper equipment is unsafe and damages heritage. Enjoy them from the valley floor.

faqs.q: Are the Mustang caves a UNESCO site?
faqs.a: The Mustang caves have been on UNESCO's tentative list since 1996, which means Nepal has put them forward for consideration, but they are not yet inscribed as a World Heritage Site. Research and conservation work continues. Check current status before you travel, as listings can change.

faqs.q: Where is Chhoser?
faqs.a: Chhoser is a small village at about 3,900 m in a valley north-east of Lo Manthang in Upper Mustang, about 1 hour by jeep or 1.5–2 hours on horseback from the walled city. It was a separate village development committee, also known as Garphu, and is now part of Lomanthang rural municipality.

faqs.q: What is Chhoser known for?
faqs.a: Chhoser is known for its cliffs full of man-made sky caves, especially the Jhong cave, a multi-level complex visitors can enter. The valley also has two cliff monasteries, Garphu and Nyiphu. It is the best place near Lo Manthang to learn about the Mustang caves and their long history of use.

faqs.q: How do I get from Lo Manthang to Chhoser?
faqs.a: By jeep in about 1 hour, on horseback in 1.5–2 hours, or on foot in about 3 hours each way. Most visitors ride or drive out in the morning and return by mid-afternoon. Jeeps and horses are arranged through lodges in Lo Manthang. Carry cash, water and a packed lunch.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Chhoser?
faqs.a: Yes. Chhoser is inside the Upper Mustang restricted area, so you need the restricted area permit, an ACAP permit and a licensed guide. Since a November 2025 decision the Upper Mustang fee is reported as USD 50 per person per day. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Chhoser worth visiting from Lo Manthang?
faqs.a: Yes. If you have two or more nights in Lo Manthang, a trip to Chhoser is the best use of a day. The Jhong cave lets you step inside a sky cave, the cliff gompas are unusual and atmospheric, and the ride across the plain is part of the experience. Allow a half day at least.

faqs.q: Is the Jhong cave difficult to explore?
faqs.a: It is not technically difficult, but it involves climbing ladders, crouching through narrow passages and moving in the dark between levels. Most reasonably fit people manage it easily with a head torch. Anyone who dislikes tight spaces can stay on the lower levels. Wear shoes with good grip.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Chhoser?
faqs.a: Chhoser has very few facilities for visitors and we do not plan overnight stays there. Lo Manthang, 1–2 hours away, has the nearest good lodges. Visiting Chhoser as a day trip from the walled city is easy, and lets you return to a warm dining room and hot food in the evening.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Chhoser?
faqs.a: May to June and September to October are best, with clear skies and comfortable temperatures. July and August are usually dry in the rain shadow, though roads from the south may be disrupted. Winter is very cold and windy, and many residents of Upper Mustang move south.

faqs.q: What should I bring to Chhoser?
faqs.a: Bring a head torch for the caves, shoes with good grip, a windproof jacket, sun hat, sunglasses, sunscreen and a buff for dust. Carry water, a packed lunch and cash in small Nepali notes for tickets and donations. If riding, a folded fleece makes the traditional saddle more comfortable.
